name: Paryushan / Das Lakshana
dateInfo: Bhadrapada Shukla Panchami to Ananta Chaturdashi (August/September)
significance: The most sacred and spiritually intense festival of the Jain calendar. Paryushan means 'to come closer' — the soul draws near to its true nature. It is a period of intense self-purification, scriptural study, fasting, Pratikramana (self-reflection), and seeking forgiveness. The 10 days represent the 10 supreme virtues (Das Lakshana) cultivated by any serious aspirant: Uttam Kshama (supreme forgiveness), Uttam Mardava (supreme humility), Uttam Arjava (supreme candor), Uttam Shauch (supreme contentment), Uttam Satya (supreme truthfulness), Uttam Sanyam (supreme self-restraint), Uttam Tap (supreme austerity), Uttam Tyaga (supreme renunciation), Uttam Akinchanya (supreme non-possession), Uttam Brahmacharya (supreme celibacy).
rituals: Puja and Abhisheka of Tirthankara idols
Scriptural recitation of Kalpa Sutra and Tattvartha Sutra
Samvatsari (annual forgiveness day) on final day
Fasting of varying intensities from 1 day to 8 days
dietaryRestrictions: Strict vegetarian, often avoiding root vegetables, green vegetables, and fruits depending on individual fasting intensity. Many observe Ayambil (restricted diet of boiled grains and pulses only).
spiritualMeaning: Paryushan is the spiritual new year's resolution: a complete reset of the soul's karmic account. Through intense self-discipline, the aspirant sheds accumulated karmas, destroys passions, renews right faith, and emerges with a completely purified consciousness, ready for the next year of spiritual progress.
audience: All Jains — from children learning first forgiveness prayers to elderly monks observing complete silence and fasting.

name: Mahavir Janma Kalyanak
significance: Celebrates the birth of Lord Mahavira (Vardhamana), the 24th and final Tirthankara, in 599 BCE at Kundagrama (Vaishali). This is one of the most widely celebrated Jain festivals, marked by joyous processions, community gatherings, temple decorations, and spiritual instruction.
rituals: Abhisheka (ceremonial bathing of baby Mahavira idol)
Special Puja with 18 essential symbols of Tirthankara
dietaryRestrictions: Strict vegetarian, Satvik (pure) food only, often avoiding tamasic (strong/fermented) items during festival period.
spiritualMeaning: The birth of Mahavira is celebrated not merely as a historical event but as a spiritual awakening for all time. Mahavira's life demonstrates that any soul can attain Kevala Jnana through 12 years of intense austerity. His teachings — Ahimsa, Satya, Aparigraha — remain the supreme guide for spiritual living. This festival re-dedicates devotees to walking the path Mahavira illuminated.
audience: All ages — children enjoy processions, youth engage in community service, adults participate in discourses, elderly practice deep meditation.

name: Diwali / Nirvana Day
significance: The most luminous day in Jain history: Lord Mahavira attained Nirvana (final liberation) on the new moon of Kartika, 527 BCE, at Pavapuri. The 18 kings of neighboring kingdoms commemorated by lighting millions of lamps — the origin of Diwali as celebrated across India. For Jains, Diwali is not merely a festival of lights but a celebration of the soul's ultimate liberation. It marks the transition from spiritual darkness to eternal light.
rituals: Lighting 108 lamps representing the path to enlightenment
Temple decoration with flowers and lights
Reading of Nirvana Kand from Kalpa Sutra
Meditation on the nature of Siddha Loka
Mental worship (mental Puja without physical offerings)
Paying respects to Acharyas and Gurus
dietaryRestrictions: Many observe complete fasting (upvas) on this day. Those who cannot fast eat only one meal (ekashana) before sunset. Clergy often observe no water (chauvihar).
spiritualMeaning: On Nirvana Day, Jains contemplate the complete cessation of suffering. The 24th Tirthankara who walked the earth for 72 years left behind no personal wealth, no empire, no army — only the path of Ahimsa. Diwali asks each person: what will you leave behind? It is a call to renunciation, simplification, and inner illumination.
audience: Universal. Householders and monks alike observe with deep reverence.

name: Bhai Beej / Bhratri Dwitiya
dateInfo: Second day of Kartika Shukla (October/November), after Diwali
significance: A festival celebrating the sacred bond between brothers and sisters, rooted in the story of Lord Neminath and his sister Rajul. When Neminath renounced the world on his wedding day, Rajul, though heartbroken, asked only that their bond continue through spiritual means. She requested he remember her in his meditation, and she would honor him through devotion. This festival honors that vow: brothers and sisters renew their commitment to protect and support each other in spiritual growth.
rituals: Sisters perform tilak and aarti for brothers
Brothers vow to protect and support sisters' spiritual practice
Exchange of gifts with spiritual significance (books, meditation cushions)
Prayers for family harmony and dharma
Reading the Bhratri Dwitiya story from scriptures
dietaryRestrictions: Normal vegetarian diet with special festive sweets prepared lovingly at home.
spiritualMeaning: In Jain tradition, the sibling relationship is sacred because it extends across lifetimes. Souls travel together through samsara, sometimes as siblings, sometimes as parents, sometimes as friends. Honoring this bond with spiritual commitment ensures both souls progress together toward liberation.
audience: Families, children, and siblings of all ages.

name: Akshay Tritiya
significance: One of the most auspicious days of the year, commemorating when Lord Rishabhdev (Adinath) broke his year-long fast (varsha tap) with sugarcane juice offered by Prince Shreyansha. This festival celebrates the fruits of perseverance in spiritual practice and the sacred act of offering (dana). It also marks the completion of the first Tirthankara's famous 400-day fast (Varshitap) — a monumental act of non-violence toward all living beings.
rituals: Breaking of Varshitap fast with sugarcane juice
Charitable donation of food and money
dietaryRestrictions: Many perform the Varshitap fast during the preceding year, eating only boiled food on alternate days or once-daily before sunset. The breaking of the fast is the festival's centerpiece.
spiritualMeaning: Akshay Tritiya teaches that spiritual effort never goes to waste — its fruits are imperishable (akshaya). A year of disciplined fasting transforms the soul, and the breaking of that fast becomes a moment of divine celebration. It inspires laypeople to undertake the Varshitap as a profound spiritual challenge.
audience: Lay Jains practicing Varshitap, families celebrating with children, and the elderly honoring tradition.

name: Jnana Panchami
significance: The festival dedicated to knowledge (Jnana). On this day, Jains worship sacred scriptures, books, and the light of wisdom. It commemorates the five supreme entities (Panch Parmeshti) who embody and propagate pure knowledge. Jains clean and honor their religious books, meditate on the 5 types of knowledge, and study scriptures with devotion. It is also known as Guru Panchami, honoring spiritual teachers.
rituals: Cleaning and worship of Jain scriptures and books
Puja with sandalwood, flowers, and lamps
Study of Tattvartha Sutra and other key texts
Respect to Gurus Acharyas and Upadhyayas
Visiting Pathshala (religious school) to honor teachers
Donation of religious texts to temples and libraries
dietaryRestrictions: Some observe partial fasting; normal vegetarian diet otherwise.
spiritualMeaning: Jnana Panchami recognizes that spiritual knowledge (Shruta Jnana) is the bridge between the seeker and liberation. The Tirthankaras are called Jinendra (conquerors of inner enemies) precisely because they possessed Ananta Jnana (infinite knowledge). Honoring books on this day is honoring the vehicle of liberation.
audience: Students, scholars, teachers, and knowledge seekers of all ages.

name: Mahavir Jayanti
significance: Celebration of Lord Mahavira's birth anniversary and his divine sermon on Ahimsa. While similar to Janma Kalyanak, some traditions mark this as the day he began his public preaching after attaining Kevala Jnana. It is a day of deep gratitude to the teacher who gave the world the systematic path of liberation through the Tri-Ratna (Three Jewels).
rituals: Grand Puja and Abhisheka to Lord Mahavira
Distribution of Prasad and charitable giving
spiritualMeaning: Mahavira did not create a new religion but purified and systematized the ancient path. His Jayanti reminds us that the teacher comes again and again to re-establish Dharma whenever it declines. Gratitude to Mahavira means following his teachings actively: non-violence in action, truth in speech, non-possession in the heart.
audience: All Jains, especially those seeking inspiration from the life of the 24th Tirthankara.

name: Kshamavani
dateInfo: Final day of Paryushan (Svetambara: Samvatsari / Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturdashi)
significance: The supreme day of forgiveness. Kshamavani (literally 'the voice of forgiveness') is when Jains seek forgiveness from every living being — explicitly or implicitly — for any harm caused in the past year. The prayer 'Khamemi Savva Jive' (I forgive all living beings) is recited, followed by 'Michchhami Dukkadam' (May all my sins be fruitless). This is the most emotionally and spiritually powerful moment in the Jain calendar.
rituals: Seeking forgiveness from family, friends, community, and Guru
Resolving to practice greater Ahimsa in the coming year
Charitable giving to monks and temples
dietaryRestrictions: Many observe complete fasting, concluding the Paryushan period with maximum austerity.
spiritualMeaning: Forgiveness is the crown jewel of Jain ethics. Kshamavani is not mere ritual — it is a profound psychological and spiritual reset. Holding onto resentment creates karmic bondage; forgiveness liberates both parties. On this day, the aspirant actively practices the highest form of Akash (space) — letting go completely, allowing the soul to breathe freely.
audience: Every Jain, regardless of age or level of practice. Children learn forgiveness; adults practice it deeply.

name: Paush Dashami
significance: Celebrates the birth of Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, in 877 BCE at Varanasi. Parshvanatha lived 250 years before Mahavira and re-established the Fourfold Jain Sangha. He is renowned for his supreme forgiveness (Kshama) — even when his teacher (or his own past-life enemy) tried to harm him repeatedly, he responded only with compassion. Paush Dashami inspires all Jains to practice forgiveness, self-control, and multi-perspective truth.
rituals: Snatra Yatra (procession of idol on chariot)
spiritualMeaning: Parshvanatha embodies Anekantavada in action. Though the 23rd Tirthankara, he respected all viewpoints and showed that spiritual truth transcends sectarian boundary. His day teaches that forgiveness is not weakness but the highest power — the power to destroy the fires of hatred.
audience: General Jain community, especially those focusing on forgiveness and patience.

name: Rohini Vrat
dateInfo: Every 27.5 days when Rohini Nakshatra rises
duration: 1 day per month (or 3 consecutive months for extended vow)
significance: A beautiful monthly fast observed by lay Jains (especially women) on the auspicious Rohini Nakshatra day. Three fasts (or 3, 5, or 7 consecutive Rohini days) are considered particularly potent. The fast involves eating only one meal before sunset, abstaining from certain foods, and dedicating the day to temple visits and scripture study. It is one of the most popular vows for married women seeking family well-being.
rituals: Fasting with a vow for spiritual merit
Puja to goddess Lakshmi and Tirthankaras
dietaryRestrictions: Single meal before sunset; strict vegetarian, no root vegetables, no evening food.
spiritualMeaning: Rohini Vrat teaches discipline through regularity. Unlike major festivals, it recurs monthly, embedding spiritual practice in the rhythm of daily life. For laywomen (and laymen who observe), it weaves spirituality into the householder's schedule, making renunciation accessible within family life.
audience: Lay Jains, especially women and families seeking spiritual discipline.

name: Navpad Oli
dateInfo: Chaitra and Ashwin Shukla Paksha (February/March and September/October)
significance: A semi-annual 9-day festival dedicated to the 9 supreme spiritual pillars (Navpad). Each day honors one of these supreme entities: Arihant, Siddha, Acharya, Upadhyaya, Sadhu, Samyak Darshana, Samyak Jnana, Samyak Charitra, and Tapa. Through meditation on these, the aspirant builds comprehensive spiritual aspiration across faith, knowledge, conduct, and austerity. It is deeply austere yet accessible through partial fasting.
rituals: Daily worship of one Navpad entity
Ayambil fasting (pure boiled food without spices, oil, dairy)
Meditation on specific spiritual quality each day
dietaryRestrictions: Ayambil is common: boiled grains only, without spices, oil, ghee, or vegetables. Some observe complete fast for all 9 days.
spiritualMeaning: Navpad Oli reinforces that the entire spiritual path is contained in these 9 supremes. By meditating on each, the aspirant builds the complete architecture of liberation. The repetition twice yearly creates powerful karmic impressions, accelerating spiritual progress.
audience: Serious householders, monks, nuns, and seekers.

name: Maun Agiyaras
dateInfo: 11th day of each month (Margashirsha month is most sacred)
significance: The festival of silence (Maun) and deep meditation. On this day, Jains observe complete silence (maun) for 24 hours — no speech, no writing, only internal spiritual practice. This silence extends beyond verbal restraint to control of mind and body. It commemorates the 11 supreme spiritual practices and the 11 stages of spiritual development. Maun Agiyaras is one of the most transformative practices in Jainism, bringing profound self-awareness.
dietaryRestrictions: Normal vegetarian diet, often with self-prepared simple food to avoid interaction.
spiritualMeaning: Speech is one of the greatest sources of karmic influx — harmful words, lies, gossip, harsh speech all create intense bandha. Complete silence on Maun Agiyaras is a radical experiment in control, revealing how much karmic energy is spent on unnecessary speech. The experience often becomes a turning point in a practitioner's spiritual life.
audience: Householders capable of 24-hour silence, youth, and monks (for whom silence is continuous).
